∅4.00 × 1.094 MK7S · drawing left, photograph right · 12 of 13 panels have a still

The same thirteen steps, each with a photograph of what the operation actually looks like. The drawings carry the geometry; the photographs carry the things a drawing cannot — how a chisel sits in a glue line, how far the tailstock comes up, what a hollow-faced block looks like under a straight edge. Every frame is cropped to the cut rather than the room, so the eye can move between drawing and photograph without hunting for the subject. Sources and timecodes are on every one.

0The part, and where it sits. ∅4.00 is reached only on the four corner arcs; the flats stay at 3.50, 0.250 inside the rim.

The finished part, sectioned on both vessels, funnel in place — pitcher left, thermos right. Path-traced from the same model the drawings come from.

The same two fits in section. On the pitcher the spigot drops into the mouth and the step lands on the rim; on the thermos the lip stands up inside the bore and the funnel’s collar clears it by 0.179. Generated at the live mark, so it cannot show an old part.

1Crosscut the 4×4: 3.50 square, 1.375 thick, dry. An END-GRAIN cookie. A 4×4 is usually boxed heart and a cookie with pith in it WILL check: seal both faces the day you cut it, and orient the blank so any check runs out at a flat, never through a corner arc.

A square blank on the faceplate with the circle scribed on it — the corners are what will come off. Wood & Shop, Bowl Blank: Square to Round, 1:10

2Bowl gouge only. The spindle roughing gouge has a narrow tang and this blank arrives as four corners a revolution — that impact is what snaps it at the ferrule.

A round-nose scraper in the hand, so the steel behind the edge is visible. The tool a sheet forbids is the one with a narrow tang at the ferrule. Beginners Guide #7, 1:20

3Glue block: dry hardwood, 1.00 thick AFTER facing — that is what the 0.30 over the screws is measured from, so start it thicker. ∅4.50, four #8 screws on a ∅2.0 circle, pilot-drilled, 0.60 deep at most. Face it on the lathe, 0.005 hollow — it seats on its rim, never rocks on a dome.

The block on the faceplate, mounted and about to be faced. Jamieson, Preparing a Glue Block, 0:48

Scraping it flat — the cut that squares the gluing face to the axis, and the reason the block exists. Same, 2:32

4Kraft paper and PVA. Scribe the block and land the square on its diagonals — the flats have to sit evenly or the arcs will not. The tailstock is the clamp. Two hours.

PVA onto the block, kraft paper laid into it. Conover, Using Paper Glue Joints, 1:18

The tailstock is the clamp; the work is spun by hand to spread the glue. Same, 2:10

5Bring the live centre up first — 4.95 across the corners on a paper joint, four impacts a revolution, and its mark gets bored away at panel 6 anyway. Then turn the corners down to ∅4.06. Lowest speed, light cuts.

The square blank turning — the tool meets wood four times a revolution until the corners are gone. Wood & Shop, 3:20

6Bore ∅2.52 through the work and 0.10 into the block — 1.475 from the face, so mark the scraper. No further: that leaves 0.30 of wood over the screws. The datum for everything after.

A round-nose scraper working END GRAIN, handle high, edge on centre. The bore in panel 6 is this cut, taken inward. Beginners Guide #7, 9:05

7Spigot ∅3.41 × 0.694 deep. The step it leaves is the face that lands on the 4.00 rim.

Cutting a step at the end of the work — the same move that leaves the spigot. Kent, 7:50

8Only the spigot end is exposed here — the flange face is glued down. Chamfer this end of the bore 45°×0.06 and sand what you can reach. The flange rim, its R0.04 and the far chamfer all wait for panel 11.

The tool presented to the face for a finishing cut. Colin Way, Turning Your First Bowl, 3:20

9OFF the lathe, flat on the bench, spindle stopped. Thin blade into the paper line and walk it right round in small bites — the arrow is your hand travelling, not the work turning. No mallet: end grain and a 0.445 wall split under impact.

The piece coming away at the paper line, clean, no fibre torn out of either face. Conover, Using Paper Glue Joints, 2:54

How he does it — mallet, work still mounted. The sheet tells you to take it off the lathe and use a thin blade instead: his piece is a thick face-grain platter, yours is a 0.445 end-grain wall. Same, 2:46

10FRESH block, same ∅4.50 × 1.00 as the first. Spigot 0.94 long — SHORTER than the bore on purpose, so the ring slides on until its face lands on the shoulder at the spigot base. Turn it OVER ∅2.52 and creep down until the ring just starts; stop at first grip.

A jam spigot being turned down on a fresh block, crept toward the fit. Kent, 10:00

11Waste disc ∅3.30 × 0.5, flat and centre-dimpled, spanning the ∅2.52 bore. IN THIS ORDER: disc on, face to 1.094 and turn the OD to ∅4.00; then retract it — it covers the bore mouth — and only then chamfer this end of the bore and round the flange rim R0.04, in light cuts.

Tool on centre with the rest set just below it — the finishing pass across a face. Colin Way, 1:40

12Check against the real objects, not the numbers. Then three thin coats of polymerised tung oil, wiped nearly dry, a day apart — bore and both faces, since it is picked up wet daily.

the fit check is made against the real pitcher, thermos and dripper — there is nothing a photograph adds
Photographs of the vessels are his own footage, 18 August. Craft frames are single stills from two woodturning videos, each credited by title and timecode, held for reference and not redistributed — the source files are gitignored. If this sheet is ever published, those frames must be replaced with footage from the garage.
Drawings generated from src/ring.py at mk7s; every dimension moves when the model moves.
